title: U.S.-Canada Trade Tensions, New PRC Extraterritorial Rules, and Russia Sanctions Approaches
transcriptText:
[music]
>> I'm Scott. I'm Bill. And we're the Trade
Guys.
You're listening to the Trade Guys, a
podcast produced by CSIS, [music]
where we talk about trade in terms that
everyone can understand. I'm Alex
Kissling, [music] and I'm here with
Scott Miller and Bill Reinsch, the CSIS
Trade Guys.
Thanks for listening to the Trade Guys.
On today's episode, Bill and Scott
discuss the latest [music] on USMCA amid
rising US-Canada trade tensions, China's
new rules targeting companies shifting
away from Chinese suppliers, and the
differing approaches taken by the United
States and [music] Europe on sanctions
against Russia.
All that and more on today's Trade Guys.
>> [music]
>> All right, Trade Guys, before we dive
into today's episode, we're going to
once again turn to Bill for a quick
update on the tariff refunds process.
Bill, I understand there's been some
news, so what's going on? Today's news
is that as a result of the last
conference with the judge, CBP
anticipates sending the first set of
refunds out on or about May 11th. So,
the wheels are turning. Okay. They have
received applications, if that's the
right word, from around 75,000 importers
of record. There are approximately
330,000 at issue, so there's a ways to
go. They are in the process of working
on more than 11 million entries, which
is more than 1/5 of what they think will
be the total. So, the system is working.
There are still reports of glitches,
people who can't get in, people who are
having password problems, people who
can't access the site, all the usual
things that happens when you try to deal
with the internet. And I don't detect
any subversive intention here. I think
this is just what happens when you're
trying to set up a new program. So, so
far, seems to be working, and it seems
to be rolling out with about as much
efficiency as you can expect from the
government. So, good news so far. Low
bar, but that's good to hear. Maybe a
dumb question, is there a deadline to
submit applications for refunds? I don't
think so, no. I mean, they may at some
point say if you don't do it by X date,
it's too late.
>> Right. But at this point, I don't think
they've suggested one. Okay. I mean,
they're hoping that a lot of people
don't apply.
Because that'll save the government
money since they put the burden on the
importers to submit data. Uh we'll see.
If you've got 330,000 people in question
here entities in question here, I
guarantee you that not all 330,000 are
going to remember to apply. No, of
course not.
>> There'll be some leakage. Of course not.
Well, we'll continue to track it. But
let's dive into our first topic today
and we're going to start with an update
on the USMCA or USMCA as we call them,
negotiations and specifically look at
the state of the US-Canada relationship
and what seems to have become a war of
words between the two countries in
recent weeks.
So, Scott, let me start with you. Where
do you think stand between the US and
Canada and where are they heading? Okay,
it's a very important question. As much
as it sounds like a lot of petty
squabbling, the US-Canada trade
relationship really matters
and the stability of that relationship,
which really in terms of free trade
agreements, goes back to the Reagan
administration when the US-Canada free
trade agreement came into effect. So,
it's a very old set of rules that have
been modified and improved over the
years, but it is rules because of the
size of the two economies and the degree
of commercial integration in companies
between US and Canada, that stable rule
set is vitally important to almost every
company that does business in North
America. So, it's way beyond just trade.
The way to think about it is Canada and
the United States
make things together and then we sell
them to each other and the rest of the
world. Mexico is added in there, too.
So, you can say that about the whole of
North America being essentially a
production unit. We make things
together, we sell them to each other in
the world, and do it in a very
competitive way, but that US Canada
relationship has been stable for a long
time. Many companies might have taken it
for granted, but nothing should be taken
for granted in this era. Okay. Now,
that's the commercial importance of
what's going on here. I think it it's
fair to say in the first time in in the
Trump administration 45 when we went
through the conversion from the worst
trade agreement ever, NAFTA, to the
best, USMCA,
about 90% of the US Canada terms and
conditions did not change. And that was
a very satisfactory outcome for many
companies. We're in a different position
now, and I think that's a reason for
some concern. First, it appears to me
that the Trump administration has
continued its preference for dealing
with Canada and Mexico separately. Yeah,
have separate issues, they're framing it
separately.
Now, over the years, Canada's been a
large trading partner, and we've had our
share of disputes. In fact, you tend to
have more fights with the people you
trade more with. That's true in the US
Canada relationship. But Canada said for
at least since 1812 or so
has had a sort of a surefire way to get
along with the US.
One is to always be strong enough to
resist the US pressures, but also at the
same time to be a relatively agreeable
and willing to talk things out, and
willing to work together to achieve
something. That second part it seems to
be missing from the relationship, and it
seems to go both ways. There's a lot of
tension, there's a lot of backbiting and
sort of nastiness in comments
on both sides. And some of it is very
petty. Airline certification
was a sort of petty bureaucratic error
that got blown up. The presence of US
wine in Canadian liquor stores has been
a thorn in the side of of the wine
producers in the US, but also continued
sort of bureaucratic pettiness. But we
don't seem to be solving problems, which
is worrisome to me.
I think the Mexico will have its own set
of issues and set of drama. That's where
China figures more significantly in how
the trade is governed between the US and
Mexico. But the US Canada relationship
appears disrupted for the wrong reasons.
Bill, how worried are you?
Well, it's hard to do this with a
straight face. This is a classic case of
life imitating art. Some of you that are
a certain age may remember John Candy's
last movie in 1995, Canadian Bacon.
And the plot of that movie is an
American president with sagging
approval ratings played by Alan Alda
decides to threaten a war with Canada in
order to boost his popularity. Does this
sound familiar at all? The movie does
not end happily for the president, by
the way, who loses the election in a
landslide.
And but it did end happily for John
Candy, who plays a sheriff in Buffalo,
who ends up saving the day, if you will,
or at least part of the day. Directed by
Michael Moore, of all people. Is that
right?
>> Yes. And there's a wonderful
anti-Canadian commercial in it about how
evil Canadians are. And it's the
voiceover announcer goes, "Canadians,
they walk among us." And they show
photos of famous Canadians like William
Shatner.
>> [laughter]
>> Alex Trebek. Alex Trebek, yeah. Michael
J. Fox. It's quite a quite
>> A roll of honor. Yes. I met with some
Canadian members of Parliament earlier
this week and they didn't have a lot to
say about the agreement. I mean, they
were mostly in in listening mode for
that. But they reminded me of something
that I hadn't thought about in a long
time, that if you think about their
history from the Canadian standpoint,
the core of it was really founded by
loyalists who opposed the American
Revolution and supported the king and
were leaving America because of that.
And fears of an American invasion were a
common thread through Canadian politics
and Canadian public opinion for at least
a century. So, a lot of people are not
entirely surprised by what's going on up
there. They're not happy, but they're
not surprised. I was a little surprised
because I thought that Trump's animosity
was based on Justin Trudeau.
And that once Trudeau was gone, things
would settle down.
Well, he's gone and they haven't settled
down. And I think it's for multiple
reasons that then we'll get back to what
Scott was talking about and the
substance. It's the one country where
Trump knows he has a whole lot of
leverage.
Geography doesn't give them a lot of
choice but to trade essentially with the
United States. Their economy is
dependent upon ours. They know it. We
know it. We're a lot bigger than they
are.
And the Trump tendency always is if you
have an advantage is to push it.
And push it as far as you possibly can.
So, that's what he's doing.
He's also dealing with the Prime
Minister who is one of the very few in
the world that stood up. Right. The
Chinese retaliated and Canada
retaliated. Not as as extensively as the
Chinese. And then Carney gave this
speech in Davos where he talked about
the need for middle powers to get
together and assert themselves.
You know, he's been kind of poking the
bear if you will.
You know, and the reality is that I
think this administration, actually most
administrations, never understand is
other countries have domestic politics,
too.
You know, it's not just us. Right. You
know, Carney's an elected leader. He has
to care about Canadian public opinion
more than he has to care about American
public opinion. And Canadian public
opinion is now is fairly solidly behind
him. There was just a poll that came out
yesterday or today that said, you know,
I think 51% think he's handling this the
right way. Which is up from mid-40s a
few weeks ago. So, the trend line there
is supportive of Carney. And I think the
signals he's getting from his voters are
that he's doing the right thing. I'm not
worried about the threat to negotiate
separately with the two countries. If
you listen to the rhetoric, there's been
a change. In the fall, there was talk
about having two separate agreements.
Most recently, Ambassador Grier has been
talking about having a separate side
letters with each country. Which
actually is quite sensible because the
issues that we have with each country
are not the same. What does that mean in
practice? Well, it means that we would
tackle individual issues through
separate bilateral discussions. The
Mexicans don't care about lumber.
And that's a huge issue with Canada. The
Canadians don't care about Mexican
tomatoes. So, a side letter would be
like an annex. Yeah. That applies only
to the two parties. Yes, it would be an
annex to the agreement. Now, it does
raise a question of kind of an
interesting question that has people
have not been talking about much yet,
which is if there is an agreement
reached, whether it would have to go
back to Congress.
And the administration has been
reluctant to send agreements to
Congress.
As was the last one. This is not a
simply a Trump thing.
My view is that if they change the rules
of origin with respect to anything, but
obviously autos being the the main
issue, that probably would require
congressional judgment because I think
the existing rules of origin are at
least referenced in the agreement. So,
they might have to go back to Congress
on that. But the side letters would
probably be a way of dealing with issues
that are uniquely bilateral. And in the
Canadian case, the big three, not in
order of importance, are lumber, dairy,
and some digital issues.
The biggest digital issue, which was
Canada's digital service tax, went away.
The Canadians bowed to Trump threats and
have gotten rid of it. But the new one
that he's worried about is provision
Canadian law that requires foreign media
to contribute to a fund that will
support the creation of Canadian media
content.
This came up in the first US-Canada Free
Trade Agreement that was negotiated in
the '80s, pre-NAFTA.
This was a big issue there. I just came
up and my boss and I at the time went to
Ottawa and one of the main topics was
Canadian cultural considerations.
And every agreement they've signed with
us is have given them a special
treatment. And there's a provision, I
think it's section 38 or 36 of USMCA
that gives them kind of a carve out to
pursue cultural initiatives. It leaves
the other two countries with some cards
to play and we're allowed to respond.
And that's what Trump is threatening
now, but that is a work out that needs
to be undertaken.
The most complicated one is probably
dairy. And as I've joked about this,
there was one 20-minute period in my
life when I understood the Canadian
dairy problem and dairy program.
Somebody from the embassy explained it
to me.
And after about 20 minutes, I lost it
and I've never recaptured it. [laughter]
The Canadian parliamentarians
acknowledge that basically what's been
going on is
they constructed what they call a supply
management program, which is a
combination of protection and government
support that guarantees a certain amount
of supply and guarantees certain amount
of that supply will be Canadian.
We took them to dispute settlement under
USMCA over this. We won.
They said they would comply. They made
some changes. We said that they had not
complied and took them back to dispute
settlement. And the second time around,
we lost. And the panel determined the
Canadians had done enough to comply.
The American view, which I think has
some merit to it, is basically what the
Canadians did and this really typifies
the relationship, is that what they did
is they found a work around. They found
a way to redefine the terms that allowed
them to award quotas that were supposed
to go to foreigners to go to Canadian
companies,
but not necessarily the same ones that
had gotten them before.
From the American point of view, this is
certainly a violation of the spirit, if
not the letter of the agreement, and
it'll be a contentious issue because
unfortunately, this is an issue where
there's a lot of politics on both sides
of the border. Yeah. Dairy is a big deal
in Ontario and a couple of the western
provinces, I think, and maybe Quebec,
too. And it's a huge deal in several
states in the United States.
>> Of course. Yeah. And presidents and
prime ministers meddle with this at
their peril. So, the negotiators have
their work cut out for us. As you'll
hear from me at greater length when we
get into USMCA next month, I really am
optimistic that all this can be worked
out with a great deal of pain, great
deal of drama, and extreme threats, but
in the end, there is a common interest
here in keeping this agreement afloat.
The consequences of tearing it apart,
which I'm sure Trump is going to
threaten to do,
the consequences they'll have actually
doing that would be devastating for all
three countries.
Probably be worse for Canada and Mexico
than it would be for us.
But, you know, what NAFTA did is create
a truly integrated North American
economy, and there's no better example
of that than the auto industry. As we'll
hear from some of our guests in the
future, if you disrupt that and start
tearing it apart, you're going to create
enormous dislocations.
And nobody wants that. None of the three
wants that. So, I think the prospects of
actually coming to an amended conclusion
with some changes is not impossible, but
to be honest about it, and I told the
Canadian parliamentarians this, Canada
does not make it easy.
They're very tough negotiators. They
don't give ground easily, and when they
do, they do it with the greatest
reluctance. And it's not going to be a
pleasant experience for either side, I'm
afraid.
Yeah, Bill, as you previewed, USMCA is
going to be a big focus of our episode
throughout the month of May. So, we'll
have much more to come on this in the
coming weeks. But, I do want to turn now
to spend a little bit of time examining
the new 18-point set of regulations
enacted earlier this month by China that
aim to penalize foreign companies for
moving supply chains outside of the
country. Bill, this was a big move that
has been heavily criticized by some in
the foreign business community. But,
give us some context on why exactly
China put these regulations in place.
And what do they do in practice?
I think the primary thing that China is
getting concerned about, and this is
only one element of these regulations
are only one element of the bigger
picture is what they're nervous about is
the building of an anti- a global
anti-China coalition. Yeah. And they see
this happening now. The overcapacity
issue has become not just a US problem
or not just a EU problem. But, it's
rapidly becoming a global problem in
developing countries all over the place.
Brazil, even South Africa, both BRICS
countries, by the way. Indonesia,
Mexico, they're all realizing that
China's export overcapacity policies
are really undermining their own
industries.
And so, there's a growing concern that
countries are going to take us on their
own already starting to take adverse
actions, mostly tariffs, against China
for these activities. This is why, for
example, China in recent months has
become the staunchest defender of the
WTO and the global trading system
because the WTO has rules that would
prevent countries from doing that. And
so, the Chinese have discovered that,
you know, it's in to their advantage to
insist on the rules. By the way, rules
that they've spent the last 20 years
ignoring. Right. But, now they are
defenders of the system because they've
realized that there's a real risk that
countries beginning with the United
States, but not limited to the United
States,
are going outside the rules to attack
them. So, I think that's the motivation.
What they're concerned with, part of
that is that companies may respond both
to the overcapacity issue as a
retaliatory measure or to the Chinese
impingements on foreign activity in
China, detaining a foreign officials,
for example, and raiding their offices.
There's been
growing number of stories about this
kind of thing that foreign firms may
respond by pulling out and altering
their supply chains by going somewhere
else.
And that's been happening. In fact, the
irony is that some Chinese companies
themselves are doing the same thing
because of the environment in China.
But that's not the target. The target is
foreign companies, and one of these
regulations gives the Chinese authority
to take action against companies that
are doing things that might, and let me
read the quote here, that might endanger
Chinese national sovereignty, security,
and development interests or harm the
legitimate rights and interests of
Chinese citizens and organizations.
That is, by the way, that's a quote, and
that's a typical Chinese regulation.
Their regulations are famous for their
ambiguity. They say, "You can't do
things that will endanger our
sovereignty."
Well, what does that mean?
You know, in most countries try to put
in the law a definition of what that
means, so companies have some idea of
what they're supposed to do and not do.
And the Chinese approach is the
opposite, which is, "We're not going to
define that in advance. We will tell you
when you have violated the rule,
and we will tell you what we're going to
do about it." And in this particular
case, one of the tools they have is to
put the company on what is called a
malicious entity list,
which then would subject the company to
penalties
such as visa restrictions, cancellations
of authorizations to work there, seizure
of property assets including digital
assets and of course fines and I think
potentially other penalties, detention
of officials and things like that. So,
what the Chinese are sort of saying is
at one level, if you try to do things
that will disrupt our economy by leaving
or cutting us out of your supply chains,
we now have a tool that will allow us to
retaliate against you.
This went into effect April 7th, so it's
too soon to say what they're going to do
with it. The other element here is the
other There's two regulations and what
the other one does is to create a
structure for countering the
extraterritorial application of other
people's laws.
And of course the prime suspect here is
the United States. Our export control
law is extraterritorial.
And we use what's called the foreign
direct product rule to argue that
products that are made somewhere else
are subject to US jurisdiction. They've
always been subject to US jurisdiction
if they're made with US parts and
components.
But now if they're made with US
technology
that makes them subject to our
jurisdiction, too.
And what the Chinese are saying is that
basically companies are going to have to
choose between being subject to Chinese
jurisdiction or being subject to foreign
jurisdiction. That they're not going to
let them walk the line here and straddle
it and they're going to say, if you
comply with an extra territorial demand
by say the United States
we're going to punish you.
And of course the United States is going
to say, if you comply with the Chinese
rules about exports, then we're going to
punish you. So, this is the worst
possible situation for business, always
has been. No matter what they do,
they're violating somebody's law. That's
right.
>> [laughter]
>> All right, I want to get Scott in here.
So, Scott, is this is this going to be
an effective move by China?
Well, it's going to have effect, but
it's going to be deadly. Look, first of
all, it's not that people are ganging up
on China or that everyone's Everyone
thinks China is a meanie. It is China is
structurally
an export-led economy with too small a
consumer sector. It's a huge economy,
but only about 40% of their GDP is
internal consumption of goods and
services by the population. In the US
and other developed economies, it's
closer to 70 or 80%. So, there's a
missing chunk in China's economy that
puts them in a position structurally
that they must export
to grow and prosper.
Those exports are causing problems
almost everywhere in the world now. So,
this is idea of overcapacity is is not
something anybody in the US made up.
It's real, and it's being felt almost
everywhere that Chinese goods are
exported, and they are very competitive
exporter, no doubt. That's first thing.
Second, if you are a company who uses
China as a point for assembly at scale
and sort of final step in production,
and then you distribute to the world,
you probably already made alternative
plans for different places to conduct
those assembly processes should worst
come to worst. The companies that will
have the most difficult time with this
regulation, in my view, are the ones who
are in China to serve the Chinese
consumer. So, take as an example Yum
Brands, Louisville, Kentucky. Famous
company, best known as Kentucky Fried
Chicken and other fine fast food. KFC is
everywhere in China.
And they're very successful brand. They
have their competitors, but they do a
great job, and they're there to serve
the needs of the Chinese customer.
And here's the catch. Almost every
single employee of Yum Brands in China
is Chinese. These are local employees
who happen to work for foreign
headquartered companies. Same with my
former employer, Procter & Gamble. It's
an international company with
headquarters in the United States, but
our China operations are almost
exclusively staffed by Chinese, in the
R&D center, in the sales organization,
at the headquarters. And so, to the
extent foreign invested enterprises are
subject to these rules, it's going to
hurt the Chinese workers who are part of
those companies, and it's the vast
majority. I don't know how that's going
to go over, but I do agree with Bill
that this sounds like a lot of Chinese
regulation, which is vague to a great
extent. It will wind up being
interpreted by a judge who's a party
official, so there's no such thing as an
independent judiciary. And they're often
structured in a way that's heads I win,
tails you lose, and there's not much
anybody can do about it. So, it has it's
ripe for abuse, and it's probably going
to be abused, and I don't know if it
achieves what the government of China
wants it to achieve because the
overcapacity is real, the remedies for
that that countries are pursuing are
going to happen. They have their own
political constituencies, and they're
going to wind up harming a lot of
Chinese employees who work for foreign
invested enterprises to serve the
Chinese customer. So, it's a tough
situation.
>> Yeah, interesting points. Well, thank
you for that. I want to turn to our
final topic today, and that's Russian
sanctions. On April 23rd, the European
Union adopted its 20th sanctions package
against Russia, with a particular focus
on the country's energy sector. At the
same time, the United States, of course,
recently allowed purchases of sanctioned
Russian oil already sitting at sea to
help ease prices during the war with
Iran. Though Treasury Secretary Scott
Bessent has since indicated that
Washington does not plan to renew that
sanctions waiver. So, Scott, I'm going
to stick with you here. We clearly have
contrasting approaches between the
United States and Europe, but how are
you viewing this? Well, I think the
release of Russian oil on the water
basically already had found an export
platform or had been loaded on a on a
tanker. I think that was a tactical step
that solved a problem of undersupply and
to calm the oil markets even if it did
it for a short period of time. I think
the broader question of you of sanctions
on Russia is what exactly have they
accomplished? And I think
the answer that I come up with
consistently is almost nothing. They
changed nothing about the sort of the
conduct of the action in Ukraine. The
financial sanctions had a big effect in
2014 and the time that the Crimean
Peninsula was being contested. And after
Crimea Russia basically crisis proofed
their system and sanction proofed it to
a great extent. And it looks to me like
well, it causes some difficulty and pain
for the target that is Russia. It
doesn't really stop them from doing much
of anything and it certainly didn't
cause financial crises or anything like
that. So, I don't know what Europe
thinks the sanctions are doing. I do
remember the title of Gary Huffbauer's
famous book on sanctions which is
feeling good versus doing good. And I
think it feels good to put more
sanctions on Russia. Separately, the
other issue here that all of this is
unaddressed is the Europe as a whole is
a massive importer of hydrocarbons.
Natural gas in particular, but also
crude oil.
>> Right. They import about as much
hydrocarbons as an entity that the EU
however many there are these days, but
that block imports about as much as we
consume in the United States of natural
gas. So, it's a big number that they're
importing somewhere from some some
source and as long as there are a
demander, there's supply or that Russia
is providing that finds a market given
these are global markets. So, I'm not
sure what they're doing. They are
demonstrating that a a desire to go in a
different direction.
Whether it's having an effect or not,
doesn't look like it to me, but Bill may
be a closer student of the the actual
sanctions and and their effect. Bill,
what's your take? Well, I think it's the
United States that's taking a slightly
different direction lately with its own
waiver. Yes. Which may or may not exist
due to expire May 16th. We'll see if it
gets extended or not. If it's not
extended, it's just a temporary blip.
And we're making much out of little in
this episode, but to me the one
noteworthy thing is this sanctions
package from the EU. This is the 20th
sanction package. Okay? They've been
consistent and steady on this
from the beginning. And I asked them
once when they were on the I don't know
eighth or 10th package, why didn't you
do everything at once? You know, it
probably would have had a bigger impact
and a bigger economic impact if you, you
know, dropped the the 100-lb hammer on
day one rather than, you know, eight
10-lb hammers.
And the answer was because we wanted the
European public not to forget about what
was going on.
And we wanted to remind them
periodically that this was still a
problem that Russia was still
invading Ukraine, still upending the
international system, and the Europeans
needed to be concerned about that. And
so, we are continually trotting out
additional sanctions packages if only to
remind the European public that this is
a problem that remains unsolved.
I thought that was interesting. I mean,
I I admire the strategy, and I think
from the standpoint of European public
opinion, that's probably had some
success.
Part of me still thinks that if they had
done it all at once, it might have had a
sharper impact on the Russians. Right.
If you look at Russia's economic data,
assuming you can believe their data,
which is always a question. Sure. I
think it's fair to say that the
sanctions collectively have had a
significant negative impact on the
Russian economy. There's no question
about that. But that has not altered
Putin's plans or it's not altered his
actions.
>> Yeah, the behavior hasn't changed at
all. No, not the objectives haven't
changed. It hasn't really affected the
war. Right. And this is the gets back to
the Hufbauer thesis. We can all pat
ourselves on the back for having done
the right thing.
But we haven't really changed anything
yet. Maybe we will. I mean, there maybe
there's a tipping point, but you know,
Russia's not a democracy anymore. People
don't get to vote in any meaningful way
to change the leadership. So, I suspect

with the waiver. I mean, it's projected

supply. As you pointed out, Scott, oil

>> A 4-year highs. And I don't see that

So, why did we do this?

I'm not sure it was it was a crazy thing

particularly in Asia. I can think of a

segments.text: [music] >> I'm Scott. I'm Bill. And we're the Trade Guys. You're listening to the Trade Guys, a podcast produced by CSIS, [music] where we talk about trade in terms that everyone can understand. I'm Alex Kissling, [music] and I'm here with

Scott Miller and Bill Reinsch, the CSIS Trade Guys. Thanks for listening to the Trade Guys. On today's episode, Bill and Scott discuss the latest [music] on USMCA amid rising US-Canada trade tensions, China's new rules targeting companies shifting

away from Chinese suppliers, and the differing approaches taken by the United States and [music] Europe on sanctions against Russia. All that and more on today's Trade Guys. >> [music] >> All right, Trade Guys, before we dive

into today's episode, we're going to once again turn to Bill for a quick update on the tariff refunds process. Bill, I understand there's been some news, so what's going on? Today's news is that as a result of the last conference with the judge, CBP

anticipates sending the first set of refunds out on or about May 11th. So, the wheels are turning. Okay. They have received applications, if that's the right word, from around 75,000 importers of record. There are approximately

330,000 at issue, so there's a ways to go. They are in the process of working on more than 11 million entries, which is more than 1/5 of what they think will be the total. So, the system is working. There are still reports of glitches,

people who can't get in, people who are having password problems, people who can't access the site, all the usual things that happens when you try to deal with the internet. And I don't detect any subversive intention here. I think

this is just what happens when you're trying to set up a new program. So, so far, seems to be working, and it seems to be rolling out with about as much efficiency as you can expect from the government. So, good news so far. Low

bar, but that's good to hear. Maybe a dumb question, is there a deadline to submit applications for refunds? I don't think so, no. I mean, they may at some point say if you don't do it by X date, it's too late. >> Right. But at this point, I don't think

they've suggested one. Okay. I mean, they're hoping that a lot of people don't apply. Because that'll save the government money since they put the burden on the importers to submit data. Uh we'll see. If you've got 330,000 people in question

here entities in question here, I guarantee you that not all 330,000 are going to remember to apply. No, of course not. >> There'll be some leakage. Of course not. Well, we'll continue to track it. But let's dive into our first topic today

and we're going to start with an update on the USMCA or USMCA as we call them, negotiations and specifically look at the state of the US-Canada relationship and what seems to have become a war of words between the two countries in recent weeks.

So, Scott, let me start with you. Where do you think stand between the US and Canada and where are they heading? Okay, it's a very important question. As much as it sounds like a lot of petty squabbling, the US-Canada trade relationship really matters

and the stability of that relationship, which really in terms of free trade agreements, goes back to the Reagan administration when the US-Canada free trade agreement came into effect. So, it's a very old set of rules that have

been modified and improved over the years, but it is rules because of the size of the two economies and the degree of commercial integration in companies between US and Canada, that stable rule set is vitally important to almost every

company that does business in North America. So, it's way beyond just trade. The way to think about it is Canada and the United States make things together and then we sell them to each other and the rest of the world. Mexico is added in there, too.

So, you can say that about the whole of North America being essentially a production unit. We make things together, we sell them to each other in the world, and do it in a very competitive way, but that US Canada relationship has been stable for a long

time. Many companies might have taken it for granted, but nothing should be taken for granted in this era. Okay. Now, that's the commercial importance of what's going on here. I think it it's fair to say in the first time in in the

Trump administration 45 when we went through the conversion from the worst trade agreement ever, NAFTA, to the best, USMCA, about 90% of the US Canada terms and conditions did not change. And that was a very satisfactory outcome for many

companies. We're in a different position now, and I think that's a reason for some concern. First, it appears to me that the Trump administration has continued its preference for dealing with Canada and Mexico separately. Yeah,

have separate issues, they're framing it separately. Now, over the years, Canada's been a large trading partner, and we've had our share of disputes. In fact, you tend to have more fights with the people you trade more with. That's true in the US

Canada relationship. But Canada said for at least since 1812 or so has had a sort of a surefire way to get along with the US. One is to always be strong enough to resist the US pressures, but also at the same time to be a relatively agreeable

and willing to talk things out, and willing to work together to achieve something. That second part it seems to be missing from the relationship, and it seems to go both ways. There's a lot of tension, there's a lot of backbiting and

sort of nastiness in comments on both sides. And some of it is very petty. Airline certification was a sort of petty bureaucratic error that got blown up. The presence of US wine in Canadian liquor stores has been a thorn in the side of of the wine

producers in the US, but also continued sort of bureaucratic pettiness. But we don't seem to be solving problems, which is worrisome to me. I think the Mexico will have its own set of issues and set of drama. That's where

China figures more significantly in how the trade is governed between the US and Mexico. But the US Canada relationship appears disrupted for the wrong reasons. Bill, how worried are you? Well, it's hard to do this with a

straight face. This is a classic case of life imitating art. Some of you that are a certain age may remember John Candy's last movie in 1995, Canadian Bacon. And the plot of that movie is an American president with sagging approval ratings played by Alan Alda

decides to threaten a war with Canada in order to boost his popularity. Does this sound familiar at all? The movie does not end happily for the president, by the way, who loses the election in a landslide. And but it did end happily for John

Candy, who plays a sheriff in Buffalo, who ends up saving the day, if you will, or at least part of the day. Directed by Michael Moore, of all people. Is that right? >> Yes. And there's a wonderful anti-Canadian commercial in it about how

evil Canadians are. And it's the voiceover announcer goes, "Canadians, they walk among us." And they show photos of famous Canadians like William Shatner. >> [laughter] >> Alex Trebek. Alex Trebek, yeah. Michael J. Fox. It's quite a quite

>> A roll of honor. Yes. I met with some Canadian members of Parliament earlier this week and they didn't have a lot to say about the agreement. I mean, they were mostly in in listening mode for that. But they reminded me of something

that I hadn't thought about in a long time, that if you think about their history from the Canadian standpoint, the core of it was really founded by loyalists who opposed the American Revolution and supported the king and were leaving America because of that.

And fears of an American invasion were a common thread through Canadian politics and Canadian public opinion for at least a century. So, a lot of people are not entirely surprised by what's going on up there. They're not happy, but they're

not surprised. I was a little surprised because I thought that Trump's animosity was based on Justin Trudeau. And that once Trudeau was gone, things would settle down. Well, he's gone and they haven't settled down. And I think it's for multiple

reasons that then we'll get back to what Scott was talking about and the substance. It's the one country where Trump knows he has a whole lot of leverage. Geography doesn't give them a lot of choice but to trade essentially with the

United States. Their economy is dependent upon ours. They know it. We know it. We're a lot bigger than they are. And the Trump tendency always is if you have an advantage is to push it. And push it as far as you possibly can. So, that's what he's doing.

He's also dealing with the Prime Minister who is one of the very few in the world that stood up. Right. The Chinese retaliated and Canada retaliated. Not as as extensively as the Chinese. And then Carney gave this speech in Davos where he talked about

the need for middle powers to get together and assert themselves. You know, he's been kind of poking the bear if you will. You know, and the reality is that I think this administration, actually most administrations, never understand is

other countries have domestic politics, too. You know, it's not just us. Right. You know, Carney's an elected leader. He has to care about Canadian public opinion more than he has to care about American public opinion. And Canadian public

opinion is now is fairly solidly behind him. There was just a poll that came out yesterday or today that said, you know, I think 51% think he's handling this the right way. Which is up from mid-40s a few weeks ago. So, the trend line there

is supportive of Carney. And I think the signals he's getting from his voters are that he's doing the right thing. I'm not worried about the threat to negotiate separately with the two countries. If you listen to the rhetoric, there's been

a change. In the fall, there was talk about having two separate agreements. Most recently, Ambassador Grier has been talking about having a separate side letters with each country. Which actually is quite sensible because the

issues that we have with each country are not the same. What does that mean in practice? Well, it means that we would tackle individual issues through separate bilateral discussions. The Mexicans don't care about lumber.

And that's a huge issue with Canada. The Canadians don't care about Mexican tomatoes. So, a side letter would be like an annex. Yeah. That applies only to the two parties. Yes, it would be an annex to the agreement. Now, it does raise a question of kind of an

interesting question that has people have not been talking about much yet, which is if there is an agreement reached, whether it would have to go back to Congress. And the administration has been reluctant to send agreements to Congress.

As was the last one. This is not a simply a Trump thing. My view is that if they change the rules of origin with respect to anything, but obviously autos being the the main issue, that probably would require congressional judgment because I think

the existing rules of origin are at least referenced in the agreement. So, they might have to go back to Congress on that. But the side letters would probably be a way of dealing with issues that are uniquely bilateral. And in the

Canadian case, the big three, not in order of importance, are lumber, dairy, and some digital issues. The biggest digital issue, which was Canada's digital service tax, went away. The Canadians bowed to Trump threats and have gotten rid of it. But the new one

that he's worried about is provision Canadian law that requires foreign media to contribute to a fund that will support the creation of Canadian media content. This came up in the first US-Canada Free Trade Agreement that was negotiated in the '80s, pre-NAFTA.

This was a big issue there. I just came up and my boss and I at the time went to Ottawa and one of the main topics was Canadian cultural considerations. And every agreement they've signed with us is have given them a special

treatment. And there's a provision, I think it's section 38 or 36 of USMCA that gives them kind of a carve out to pursue cultural initiatives. It leaves the other two countries with some cards to play and we're allowed to respond.

And that's what Trump is threatening now, but that is a work out that needs to be undertaken. The most complicated one is probably dairy. And as I've joked about this, there was one 20-minute period in my life when I understood the Canadian

dairy problem and dairy program. Somebody from the embassy explained it to me. And after about 20 minutes, I lost it and I've never recaptured it. [laughter] The Canadian parliamentarians acknowledge that basically what's been going on is

they constructed what they call a supply management program, which is a combination of protection and government support that guarantees a certain amount of supply and guarantees certain amount of that supply will be Canadian.

We took them to dispute settlement under USMCA over this. We won. They said they would comply. They made some changes. We said that they had not complied and took them back to dispute settlement. And the second time around,

we lost. And the panel determined the Canadians had done enough to comply. The American view, which I think has some merit to it, is basically what the Canadians did and this really typifies the relationship, is that what they did

is they found a work around. They found a way to redefine the terms that allowed them to award quotas that were supposed to go to foreigners to go to Canadian companies, but not necessarily the same ones that had gotten them before.

From the American point of view, this is certainly a violation of the spirit, if not the letter of the agreement, and it'll be a contentious issue because unfortunately, this is an issue where there's a lot of politics on both sides

of the border. Yeah. Dairy is a big deal in Ontario and a couple of the western provinces, I think, and maybe Quebec, too. And it's a huge deal in several states in the United States. >> Of course. Yeah. And presidents and prime ministers meddle with this at

their peril. So, the negotiators have their work cut out for us. As you'll hear from me at greater length when we get into USMCA next month, I really am optimistic that all this can be worked out with a great deal of pain, great

deal of drama, and extreme threats, but in the end, there is a common interest here in keeping this agreement afloat. The consequences of tearing it apart, which I'm sure Trump is going to threaten to do, the consequences they'll have actually

doing that would be devastating for all three countries. Probably be worse for Canada and Mexico than it would be for us. But, you know, what NAFTA did is create a truly integrated North American economy, and there's no better example

of that than the auto industry. As we'll hear from some of our guests in the future, if you disrupt that and start tearing it apart, you're going to create enormous dislocations. And nobody wants that. None of the three wants that. So, I think the prospects of

actually coming to an amended conclusion with some changes is not impossible, but to be honest about it, and I told the Canadian parliamentarians this, Canada does not make it easy. They're very tough negotiators. They don't give ground easily, and when they

do, they do it with the greatest reluctance. And it's not going to be a pleasant experience for either side, I'm afraid. Yeah, Bill, as you previewed, USMCA is going to be a big focus of our episode throughout the month of May. So, we'll

have much more to come on this in the coming weeks. But, I do want to turn now to spend a little bit of time examining the new 18-point set of regulations enacted earlier this month by China that aim to penalize foreign companies for

moving supply chains outside of the country. Bill, this was a big move that has been heavily criticized by some in the foreign business community. But, give us some context on why exactly China put these regulations in place. And what do they do in practice?

I think the primary thing that China is getting concerned about, and this is only one element of these regulations are only one element of the bigger picture is what they're nervous about is the building of an anti- a global

anti-China coalition. Yeah. And they see this happening now. The overcapacity issue has become not just a US problem or not just a EU problem. But, it's rapidly becoming a global problem in developing countries all over the place.

Brazil, even South Africa, both BRICS countries, by the way. Indonesia, Mexico, they're all realizing that China's export overcapacity policies are really undermining their own industries. And so, there's a growing concern that

countries are going to take us on their own already starting to take adverse actions, mostly tariffs, against China for these activities. This is why, for example, China in recent months has become the staunchest defender of the

WTO and the global trading system because the WTO has rules that would prevent countries from doing that. And so, the Chinese have discovered that, you know, it's in to their advantage to insist on the rules. By the way, rules

that they've spent the last 20 years ignoring. Right. But, now they are defenders of the system because they've realized that there's a real risk that countries beginning with the United States, but not limited to the United States,

are going outside the rules to attack them. So, I think that's the motivation. What they're concerned with, part of that is that companies may respond both to the overcapacity issue as a retaliatory measure or to the Chinese impingements on foreign activity in

China, detaining a foreign officials, for example, and raiding their offices. There's been growing number of stories about this kind of thing that foreign firms may respond by pulling out and altering their supply chains by going somewhere else.

And that's been happening. In fact, the irony is that some Chinese companies themselves are doing the same thing because of the environment in China. But that's not the target. The target is foreign companies, and one of these

regulations gives the Chinese authority to take action against companies that are doing things that might, and let me read the quote here, that might endanger Chinese national sovereignty, security, and development interests or harm the

legitimate rights and interests of Chinese citizens and organizations. That is, by the way, that's a quote, and that's a typical Chinese regulation. Their regulations are famous for their ambiguity. They say, "You can't do things that will endanger our

sovereignty." Well, what does that mean? You know, in most countries try to put in the law a definition of what that means, so companies have some idea of what they're supposed to do and not do. And the Chinese approach is the

opposite, which is, "We're not going to define that in advance. We will tell you when you have violated the rule, and we will tell you what we're going to do about it." And in this particular case, one of the tools they have is to

put the company on what is called a malicious entity list, which then would subject the company to penalties such as visa restrictions, cancellations of authorizations to work there, seizure of property assets including digital

assets and of course fines and I think potentially other penalties, detention of officials and things like that. So, what the Chinese are sort of saying is at one level, if you try to do things that will disrupt our economy by leaving

or cutting us out of your supply chains, we now have a tool that will allow us to retaliate against you. This went into effect April 7th, so it's too soon to say what they're going to do with it. The other element here is the

other There's two regulations and what the other one does is to create a structure for countering the extraterritorial application of other people's laws. And of course the prime suspect here is the United States. Our export control law is extraterritorial.

And we use what's called the foreign direct product rule to argue that products that are made somewhere else are subject to US jurisdiction. They've always been subject to US jurisdiction if they're made with US parts and components.

But now if they're made with US technology that makes them subject to our jurisdiction, too. And what the Chinese are saying is that basically companies are going to have to choose between being subject to Chinese jurisdiction or being subject to foreign

jurisdiction. That they're not going to let them walk the line here and straddle it and they're going to say, if you comply with an extra territorial demand by say the United States we're going to punish you. And of course the United States is going

to say, if you comply with the Chinese rules about exports, then we're going to punish you. So, this is the worst possible situation for business, always has been. No matter what they do, they're violating somebody's law. That's right. >> [laughter]

>> All right, I want to get Scott in here. So, Scott, is this is this going to be an effective move by China? Well, it's going to have effect, but it's going to be deadly. Look, first of all, it's not that people are ganging up

on China or that everyone's Everyone thinks China is a meanie. It is China is structurally an export-led economy with too small a consumer sector. It's a huge economy, but only about 40% of their GDP is internal consumption of goods and

services by the population. In the US and other developed economies, it's closer to 70 or 80%. So, there's a missing chunk in China's economy that puts them in a position structurally that they must export to grow and prosper.

Those exports are causing problems almost everywhere in the world now. So, this is idea of overcapacity is is not something anybody in the US made up. It's real, and it's being felt almost everywhere that Chinese goods are

exported, and they are very competitive exporter, no doubt. That's first thing. Second, if you are a company who uses China as a point for assembly at scale and sort of final step in production, and then you distribute to the world,

you probably already made alternative plans for different places to conduct those assembly processes should worst come to worst. The companies that will have the most difficult time with this regulation, in my view, are the ones who

are in China to serve the Chinese consumer. So, take as an example Yum Brands, Louisville, Kentucky. Famous company, best known as Kentucky Fried Chicken and other fine fast food. KFC is everywhere in China. And they're very successful brand. They

have their competitors, but they do a great job, and they're there to serve the needs of the Chinese customer. And here's the catch. Almost every single employee of Yum Brands in China is Chinese. These are local employees who happen to work for foreign

headquartered companies. Same with my former employer, Procter & Gamble. It's an international company with headquarters in the United States, but our China operations are almost exclusively staffed by Chinese, in the R&D center, in the sales organization,

at the headquarters. And so, to the extent foreign invested enterprises are subject to these rules, it's going to hurt the Chinese workers who are part of those companies, and it's the vast majority. I don't know how that's going

to go over, but I do agree with Bill that this sounds like a lot of Chinese regulation, which is vague to a great extent. It will wind up being interpreted by a judge who's a party official, so there's no such thing as an

independent judiciary. And they're often structured in a way that's heads I win, tails you lose, and there's not much anybody can do about it. So, it has it's ripe for abuse, and it's probably going to be abused, and I don't know if it

achieves what the government of China wants it to achieve because the overcapacity is real, the remedies for that that countries are pursuing are going to happen. They have their own political constituencies, and they're going to wind up harming a lot of

Chinese employees who work for foreign invested enterprises to serve the Chinese customer. So, it's a tough situation. >> Yeah, interesting points. Well, thank you for that. I want to turn to our final topic today, and that's Russian

sanctions. On April 23rd, the European Union adopted its 20th sanctions package against Russia, with a particular focus on the country's energy sector. At the same time, the United States, of course, recently allowed purchases of sanctioned

Russian oil already sitting at sea to help ease prices during the war with Iran. Though Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent has since indicated that Washington does not plan to renew that sanctions waiver. So, Scott, I'm going

to stick with you here. We clearly have contrasting approaches between the United States and Europe, but how are you viewing this? Well, I think the release of Russian oil on the water basically already had found an export platform or had been loaded on a on a

tanker. I think that was a tactical step that solved a problem of undersupply and to calm the oil markets even if it did it for a short period of time. I think the broader question of you of sanctions on Russia is what exactly have they

accomplished? And I think the answer that I come up with consistently is almost nothing. They changed nothing about the sort of the conduct of the action in Ukraine. The financial sanctions had a big effect in 2014 and the time that the Crimean

Peninsula was being contested. And after Crimea Russia basically crisis proofed their system and sanction proofed it to a great extent. And it looks to me like well, it causes some difficulty and pain for the target that is Russia. It

doesn't really stop them from doing much of anything and it certainly didn't cause financial crises or anything like that. So, I don't know what Europe thinks the sanctions are doing. I do remember the title of Gary Huffbauer's

famous book on sanctions which is feeling good versus doing good. And I think it feels good to put more sanctions on Russia. Separately, the other issue here that all of this is unaddressed is the Europe as a whole is a massive importer of hydrocarbons.

Natural gas in particular, but also crude oil. >> Right. They import about as much hydrocarbons as an entity that the EU however many there are these days, but that block imports about as much as we consume in the United States of natural

gas. So, it's a big number that they're importing somewhere from some some source and as long as there are a demander, there's supply or that Russia is providing that finds a market given these are global markets. So, I'm not sure what they're doing. They are

demonstrating that a a desire to go in a different direction. Whether it's having an effect or not, doesn't look like it to me, but Bill may be a closer student of the the actual sanctions and and their effect. Bill, what's your take? Well, I think it's the

United States that's taking a slightly different direction lately with its own waiver. Yes. Which may or may not exist due to expire May 16th. We'll see if it gets extended or not. If it's not extended, it's just a temporary blip.

And we're making much out of little in this episode, but to me the one noteworthy thing is this sanctions package from the EU. This is the 20th sanction package. Okay? They've been consistent and steady on this from the beginning. And I asked them

once when they were on the I don't know eighth or 10th package, why didn't you do everything at once? You know, it probably would have had a bigger impact and a bigger economic impact if you, you know, dropped the the 100-lb hammer on

day one rather than, you know, eight 10-lb hammers. And the answer was because we wanted the European public not to forget about what was going on. And we wanted to remind them periodically that this was still a problem that Russia was still

invading Ukraine, still upending the international system, and the Europeans needed to be concerned about that. And so, we are continually trotting out additional sanctions packages if only to remind the European public that this is

a problem that remains unsolved. I thought that was interesting. I mean, I I admire the strategy, and I think from the standpoint of European public opinion, that's probably had some success. Part of me still thinks that if they had

done it all at once, it might have had a sharper impact on the Russians. Right. If you look at Russia's economic data, assuming you can believe their data, which is always a question. Sure. I think it's fair to say that the sanctions collectively have had a

significant negative impact on the Russian economy. There's no question about that. But that has not altered Putin's plans or it's not altered his actions. >> Yeah, the behavior hasn't changed at all. No, not the objectives haven't

changed. It hasn't really affected the war. Right. And this is the gets back to the Hufbauer thesis. We can all pat ourselves on the back for having done the right thing. But we haven't really changed anything yet. Maybe we will. I mean, there maybe

there's a tipping point, but you know, Russia's not a democracy anymore. People don't get to vote in any meaningful way to change the leadership. So, I suspect it's not going to have an immediate impact. I still am baffled though, and

maybe Scott can comment on this. I'm not entirely sure why the US did what it did with the waiver. I mean, it's projected to produce an increase in Russian revenue, oil company revenue, of up to $200 million a day, which is not peanuts.

And we're giving them this sort of gift. And I I don't quite understand why. I mean, it doesn't seem to me it's having that much of an effect on global oil supply. As you pointed out, Scott, oil prices have reached record highs now.

>> A 4-year highs. And I don't see that coming down because of Russian supply. So, why did we do this? It was I believe it was an attempt to stabilize oil prices when they were spiking. And it may or may not have done that, but it did provide more supply on

the market and there is a supply shortage because of the restrictions on Iran's exports. So, there was an attempt to balance it and that's probably the least negative of all options. There aren't a whole lot of good options when

it comes to those kinds of actions. So, I'm not sure it was it was a crazy thing to do or an ineffective thing to do given that there are major hydrocarbon shortages particularly in Asia. I can think of a good option, which is stop the blockade.

Well, yes, we could do that. But in the realm of the actions that are being considered now, that this one didn't seem particularly harmful to me. It was done judiciously in terms of affecting oil that had already been produced and was in in transit and it

had an end point. So, I don't see it as a catastrophic error on anybody's part. Energy's a huge market and this is a disruption to it. The war is a disruption to it in general. >> Yeah. We got to live with that. The impact at the margin, I don't think the

impact is significant. What worries me about it is it does suggest a divergence in US and European goals and that that worries me. I mean, the Europeans have been consistent on this. Well, that's but that's true of the entire

operation. I mean, look at Europe's response to keeping the the straits open. It's been difficult with Europe on all matters in in this war. So, this is only one. Fair point. All right, we ended on agreement. On a topic where

we started with contrasting views, we have agreement between Bill and Scott. We do that on more occasions than you might think. It's a good day. All right, guys, we're going to leave it there. Thanks so much to all of our listeners

for joining us. Bill and Scott, thank you as always and we will be back with you next week. Take care until then. Thank you. Thank you. You've been listening to the Trade [music] Guys, a CSIS podcast. For more audio content, visit csis.org/podcast.
Thanks for tuning in. >> [music]
